newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major defends EMU policy, won't sack rebels.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major defends EMU policy, won't sack rebels.

text.p: Britain's election campaign sprang to life on Wednesday when Prime Minister John Major made his most passionate defence yet of why he would not rule out entering the European Union's planned single currency.
But Major left himself open to opposition accusations of weak leadership by making it clear he would not sack two junior ministers who have openly defied his "wait and see" stance.
Divisions in the ruling Conservative Party over Europe have dogged Major's 6-1/2 years in power and were always likely to come to the forefront of the May 1 election campaign.

When they did so on Wednesday, with newspapers splashing on the opposition of junior ministers John Horam and James Paice to any move to scrap the pound sterling, Major tackled the issue head-on with an eloquent exposition of the pros and cons of monetary union and of why he needed to keep his options open.
"I will negotiate in the interests of the United Kingdom as a whole, not in the convenient party political interests of the Conservative Party," he told a news conference.
"If that is unhappy politically for some, then I regret that...but I have to answer to my conscience and my nation and history for what I actually decide to do on this matter."
Major said that to rule out any options now, on an issue that was the most important in generations, would be to send him naked into the negotiating chamber.
"Like me or loath me, do not bind my hands when I am negotiating on behalf of the British nation," he said.
But when asked whether he would sack Horam and Paice for breaking ranks, Major effectively said he would not.

"We have spoken to those two ministers overnight. They realise how unwise they were. They realise that they have to accept our negotiate-and-decide policy. They realise that they are bound by collective responsibility," he said.
The main opposition Labour Party, hot favourite according to opinion polls to return to power for the first time since 1979, pounced on Major's reply.

"Britain cannot be represented by a government with all the leadership qualities of lemmings. Britain cannot be represented by a government that is fighting among themselves and therefore they cannot fight for Britain," Labour leader Tony Blair said in Southampton, southern England.

"We are witnessing the collapse of the Conservative Party under the weight of its own divisions. We are seeing the culmination of six years of weak leadership, a prime minister reduced to a laughing stock by his members of parliament, his party now a rabble," Blair added.
Major said fundamental questions about the single currency, due to be launched in 1999, still had to be answered.
He said it would be folly to rule out joining a project that, if it worked, would boost living standards. To stay out could also threaten the flow of foreign investment into Britain.

Equally, to enter a flawed monetary union would be an economic catastrophe beyond calculation. Scrapping the pound, moreover, might be the prelude to the transfer of tax and spending policies to Brussels, which would be unacceptable.

"Can anybody honestly put their hand on their heart and say that they know for certain what the outcome would be if we were to decide now, precipitately, without the details at this moment, that never in any circumstances were we going to decide to enter a European single currency?
"Can anybody truly know the answer to that question? I do not believe that anybody can honestly say they do," Major said.
With the spotlight on Europe, more sparkling economic figures published on Wednesday were largely overlooked.

The number of people recorded as out of work and claiming jobless benefit fell by 41,100 to 1.71 million in March, a 6-1/2 year low. Growth in average annual earnings picked up to five percent and the annual budget deficit came in under target.
Major said the figures showed Britain was booming thanks to Conservative policies. Labour said the job figures were fiddled.
